Objective for processing:  
The main objectives for this project are: 
1) To improve clinical outcomes by better reporting of hospital and community acquired Acute Kidney Injury (AKI) at regional and CCG level
2) To understand demographic, socioeconomic and factors affecting regional variation in incidence and case-fatality of AKI.
3) To understand long-term clinical outcomes after AKI in terms of development of chronic kidney disease and mortality
The researchers would like to investigate some specific questions: 
1. To investigate the long-term outcome of AKI in community and hospitals at Trust, regional and CCG levels. Expected output: Peer-reviewed publication and new hypotheses for future research – 18-24 months.
2. To investigate the cause for variation in the mortality of AKI. Expected output: Peer-reviewed publication and new hypotheses for future research - 12-18 months.
3. To explore variation in dialysis-requiring AKI in various hospital Trusts. Expected output: Peer-reviewed publication and new hypotheses for future research; evidence to support a future grant application aimed at improving survival on dialysis - 12-24 months.  
4. To explore hospital readmission rates and bed usage for all AKI. Rates will be investigated in different demographic groups and renal-center specific standardized admission rates produced. Expected output: Peer-reviewed publication and new hypotheses for future research - 12-24 months.
The Trust believes this study will give the most accurate estimates to date of incidence and case fatality rate of AKI as the primary reason for hospital admission in England. These data will allow lay people, the medical community and healthcare policy makers to appreciate the true burden of this important disease. This is important because it is the first critical step in developing strategies to reduce the incidence of AKI as well as improve outcomes. As such this study is well aligned with initiatives undertaken by NHS England to better understand the burden of AKI in England with the goal of developing national initiatives to reduce the incidence and improve survival.
There is some evidence emerging from single centre studies and studies from selected locations, that long-term outcomes of AKI requiring dialysis are poor and many patient require long-term dialysis. In addition, there is some evidence that AKI leads to increase cardiovascular mortality. However, there is no evidence from England and more so, there is no evidence for above from large scale national data. The knowledge gained from this study will identify variation in mortality and the determinants of this variation. 
The HSCIC data has region as one variable and the Trust will be able to study the variation in 9 different regions of England. The data provided by ONS will be used to calculate population incidence of AKI in each region. The data will also be useful to study centers that currently do not have provision of renal replacement therapy.

Processing activities: 
The data will be analysed to study long-term outcome – Renal as well as patient outcome (survival) over a period of 15 years, broken down by demographic and regional areas. The data will provide date of death. The Trust will calculate the time on survival (days/months) and use statistical analysis (cox proportional hazard analysis and Kaplan Meir survival analysis) to plot and compare survival in different age groups and region. 
The Trust will also request linkage to other dataset like UKRR (UK Renal Registry) dataset to study the progression of AKI into Chronic Kidney Disease (CKD).  This is not included in this application and will be subject to a future application at a later date. This will take the form of a request made by the Trust to the UKRR for them to send identifiers from the UKRR dataset to the HSCIC. The linkage would then be performed by the HSCIC and a pseudonymised output then returned back to the Trust.
No patient identifiable data will be used for analysis and publishing. 

Specific outputs expected, including target date: 
For each of the aforementioned objectives, the research outcomes will also be disseminated via:
a)	Oral and/or poster presentations at national and international renal meetings.
b)	Publications in peer-reviewed clinical journals
As mortality can be high after discharge in AKI, the Trust plan to assess mortality at 30, 60 and 90-day from day of discharge and long-term mortality with specific examination of the factors which affect mortality. 
The analysis is expected to be completed by June 2016 depending on the availability of the linked HES+ONS data. 
The Trust will publish and disseminate findings in peer-reviewed journal to improve overall care for AKI patients. The journals targeted are British Medical Journal, Nephrology Dialysis and Transplantation, Clinical Journal of American Society of Nephrology.
The analysis of the data will be presented in scientific meetings (British Renal Society, Renal Association, UK, European Renal Association and American Society of Nephrology) and in peer reviewed journals- British Medical Journal, Nephrology Dialysis and Transplantation, Clinical Journal of American Society of Nephrology. 
In addition, the results of the analysis will be shared with National Kidney Federation and AKI Clinical Study Group (AKI-CSG) who have supported this research. The AKI-CSG has given their support for the study. The National Kidney Federation have not funded this research but are supportive of it and will be presented with the results of the analysis.
All outputs will only contain aggregated data (with small numbers suppressed in line with the HES analysis guide).

Expected measurable benefits to health and/or social care including target date: 
Benefits aimed to be achieved by working on research question 1 (above):
England will be the first country to report accurately the incidence and case-fatality from AKI at national, regional and CCG level from ICD-10 coded definition of AKI. Anecdotal evidence indicates that long-term outcome of dialysis requiring AKI is poor, though there is no evidence for this from England. This study will provide evidence of long-term outcomes after patient is discharged and will be useful for service planning at national level by clinicians and commissioners who will view the findings through peer-reviewed publications. The results will be presented at scientific meetings – Renal Association, British Renal Society and also in AKI meeting of Strategic Clinical Network. Target: 12-18 months
Benefits aimed to be achieved by working on research question 2 (above):
Knowledge gained about regional variation in the mortality of dialysis requiring AKI will help to identify areas with unusual variations. This will be viewed by Trusts, GP practices and commissioners via peer-reviewed publications and used to identify knowledge and service gaps and a targeted approach involving service configuration and educational tools. The results will be presented at scientific meetings – Renal Association, British Renal Society and also in AKI meeting of Strategic. Target: 12-18 months
Benefits aimed to be achieved by working on research question 3 (above):
Clinicians will gain a better understanding of the factors associated with variation in severe form of AKI requiring dialysis and this will help service planning as not all hospitals have the facility to offer renal replacement therapy. In addition, a better understanding of factors which lead to progression from milder forms of AKI to severe forms requiring Renal Replacement Treatment (RRT) will help to reduce progression of AKI, length of stay and mortality. The data will also provide a strong evidence base for grant applications and support the case for funding. The results will be presented in peer-reviewed journals and at scientific meetings – Renal Association, British Renal Society and also in AKI meeting of Strategic Clinical Network. Target: 12-24 months
Benefits aimed to be achieved by working on research question 4 (above):
Anecdotal evidence from single centre studies suggests that length of stay and readmission rates are high in dialysis requiring AKI patients. With analyses of the linked data set (for which the Trust are requesting this permission), difference between region specific rates will be available for the first time. The results will be presented at scientific meeting – Renal Association, British Renal Society and also in AKI meeting of Strategic The linked dataset will be used by clinicians and commissioners to identify best practice and set a benchmark for future improvements and will inform strategies that lead to a reduction in overall hospitalization rates. Target: 12-24 months 
There is increasing evidence that AKI episodes, transient and permanent, lead to increased risk of end stage renal disease and all-cause mortality. The linked data with HES and UKRR will provide longitudinal data confirming and quantifying this relationship. Intervention studies initiated in selected locations in England can help understand the effectiveness and help prevent progression of AKI.
In summary, the Trust expect the benefits to include further published work in peer-reviewed medical journals, strategic clinical networks and scientific meetings like Renal Association and British Renal Society and further findings which may lead to quality improvement initiatives
